title: The Closed Hand
logline: A family workshop takes on an apprentice from outside the family. The craft passes hand to hand in daily lessons, but some steps are only ever done when the apprentice has gone home.

object.note: Object 3 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: What is held back moves from the catch to a skill: a family workshop that teaches an outsider, but not everything.

thread_out.thread: From a workshop's slow, private tension to an hour of shared heat by a roadside: a broken-down bus and strangers whose mood shifts more than once.

requirements: A hereditary craft workshop currently training an apprentice from outside the family
Consent from the family to show what they are comfortable showing, and no more
An apprentice willing to speak about their own experience of the teaching

suggestions.name: A family brass or metalwork workshop
suggestions.why: A region with a long-standing tradition of hereditary metal-craft workshops, some still family-run and training-based.
suggestions.verify: A specific workshop currently training an outside apprentice must be found and confirmed; this is a region-level suggestion only.

lesson.in_simple_terms: People can be possessive about a skill just as much as about money or land. The texts count knowledge among the things a mind can hold back, and describe that holding back as a kind of discomfort at sharing.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: මුදල්, ඉඩකඩම් ගැන මෙන්ම තමා දන්නා ශිල්පයක් ගැනද මසුරුකම ඇතිවිය හැකි බවත්, එය බෙදාදීමට ඇති අකමැත්තක් ලෙස පෙනෙන බවත් ධර්මය කියයි.
lesson.the_teaching: Both texts name five kinds of stinginess (macchariya): over one's dwelling, family, gain, praise, and knowledge or teaching (dhamma), so a skill one knows is as much a possible object of this holding back as a house or an income. It belongs to the 'hate tetrad', the factors that arise only in the two hate-rooted minds. Margaya explains why: though born of attachment to one's own, stinginess shows itself as displeasure at sharing, so it sits with aversion rather than with greed.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The viewer learns the craft alongside the apprentice, at exactly the pace the apprentice is allowed to learn it. Open demonstrations sit beside the moments the apprentice is sent home, and the family's own quiet talk about how much to show lets the viewer feel the pull between protecting a livelihood and passing a skill on, without the film deciding which it is.

key_terms.en: the hate tetrad (hate, envy, stinginess, remorse)

lesson.caution: This does not mean a family guarding its craft is doing wrong; protecting a livelihood can look the same from outside, and no camera can show which state of mind is present.
lesson.builds_on: The even share showed holding back over a catch; this film moves the same pull from fish to knowledge, which the texts count as one more thing a mind can keep to itself.
lesson.evidence_class: editorial interpretation grounded in cited source teaching
